stem: Before a maintenance hemodialysis treatment, the nurse compares the client's current weight with the prescribed target dry weight. Why is this comparison clinically important?

options.A: It helps estimate fluid gained between treatments and informs fluid-removal planning together with blood pressure, symptoms, urine output, and treatment tolerance.
options.B: It is used to set the fluid-removal amount from the weight difference alone, with blood pressure and symptoms assessed after the dialysis session is completed.
options.C: It mainly measures long-term nutritional body-mass change, while dialysis fluid removal is planned from blood pressure and urine output rather than weight gain.
options.D: It is primarily a measure of dialysis solute clearance, so the weight comparison can be used in place of other measures of treatment effectiveness such as laboratory results.

rationale: The National Kidney Foundation defines dry weight as body weight without excess fluid and explains that extra fluid accumulates between dialysis treatments. NKF guidance on ultrafiltration states that dialysis staff set the ultrafiltration rate based on fluid weight gain since the prior treatment. Current NKF hemodialysis guidance also emphasizes that the team considers how much fluid needs removal together with blood pressure, symptoms, residual urine output, and treatment tolerance because removing too much fluid too quickly can cause complications. Therefore A is correct. B overrelies on weight alone and delays other assessment. C mischaracterizes the purpose of the comparison. D confuses fluid-volume planning with measures of solute clearance.
educational_objective: Use the pre-dialysis weight relative to target dry weight to estimate interdialytic fluid accumulation and support ultrafiltration planning while integrating blood pressure, symptoms, residual urine output, and treatment tolerance.
source_document_title: What Is Dry Weight?; Ultrafiltration; Hemodialysis: How It Works, Types, and What to Expect
source_version_date: Dry-weight and ultrafiltration guidance current 2026; Hemodialysis last updated July 24, 2026
source_locator: What Is Dry Weight? > What is dry weight?: dry weight is weight without extra fluid; fluid and wastes build up between treatments; there is a limit to how much fluid can safely be removed in one treatment. Ultrafiltration > Ultrafiltration in Hemodialysis: ultrafiltration removes fluid and staff set the ultrafiltration rate based on fluid weight gain since the last treatment. Hemodialysis > How your dialysis team checks if treatment is working: assessment includes how much fluid needs removal, blood pressure before/during/after treatment, lab results and symptoms, and whether the client still makes urine; Side effects/safety: removing too much fluid too quickly can cause cramps, dizziness, nausea, headache, or hypotension.
source_claim_supported: Comparing current weight with target dry weight helps estimate excess fluid accumulated between treatments and informs ultrafiltration planning, but safe fluid removal also requires broader clinical assessment and treatment-tolerance data.

supporting_sources.locator: Ultrafiltration in Hemodialysis: ultrafiltration removes fluid through the dialysis membrane; ultrafiltration rate and dialysis time control the amount removed; staff set the rate based on fluid weight gain since the last treatment.
supporting_sources.claim_supported: Interdialytic fluid weight gain directly informs the prescribed ultrafiltration rate.

supporting_sources.document_title: Hemodialysis: How It Works, Types, and What to Expect
supporting_sources.locator: How your dialysis team checks if treatment is working; Side effects/symptoms of dialysis and safety.
supporting_sources.claim_supported: Dialysis fluid-management assessment includes fluid-removal need, blood pressure, symptoms, residual urine output, and tolerance; overly rapid removal can cause adverse symptoms and hypotension.

correction_summary: Rebuilt all four options to remove absolute-word cueing and the very long keyed answer, preserved the dry-weight/ultrafiltration construct, added clinically realistic misconceptions about single-measurement reliance and solute clearance, and remapped the item to the direct NCSBN Physiological Adaptation hemodialysis and fluid-balance statements.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Hemodialysis — dry weight, interdialytic fluid gain, and ultrafiltration planning
audit_findings.stem: PASS — specifies maintenance hemodialysis and a comparison with prescribed target dry weight without assuming a fixed ultrafiltration formula.
audit_findings.option_A: PASS — directly reflects current NKF guidance on fluid weight gain plus the broader clinical assessment required for safe treatment; uniquely best.
audit_findings.option_B: PASS as distractor — the weight difference is important, but relying on it alone and delaying blood-pressure/symptom assessment conflicts with safe dialysis monitoring.
audit_findings.option_C: PASS as distractor — true body-mass changes can affect dry-weight reassessment, but the immediate pre-dialysis comparison is directly relevant to excess fluid and fluid-removal planning.
audit_findings.option_D: PASS as distractor — weight trends inform fluid management, while solute clearance is assessed through other treatment and laboratory measures.
audit_findings.ambiguity: PASS — A is the only option that accurately states both the value and the limitations of the weight comparison.
audit_findings.second_answer: EXCLUDED — B overrelies on a single measure, C misidentifies the primary immediate use, and D confuses fluid-volume assessment with solute clearance.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — all options are tightly matched in length and complexity; the keyed answer is not the longest and no keyed-only absolute wording remains.
audit_findings.blueprint: PASS — NCSBN Physiological Adaptation directly includes hemodialysis management and fluid/electrolyte imbalance management.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — challenged whether weight difference alone could reasonably determine ultrafiltration; NKF explicitly links ultrafiltration rate to fluid weight gain but separately requires assessment of blood pressure, symptoms, residual urine and tolerance, leaving A uniquely complete.
